claim: The generation-interval distribution plays a key role in determining the spread and control of emerging epidemics such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The generation-interval distribution plays a key role in determining the spread and control of emerging epidemics such as the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of generation-interval distribution in epidemiology, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: At the population level, the generation-interval distribution links incidence of infection, particularly the epidemic growth rate r, with the reproduction number R.
source: At the population level, the generation-interval distribution links incidence of infection, particularly the epidemic growth rate r, with the reproduction number R (Gostic et al., 2020; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gostic et al., 2020; Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007).

claim: Short generation intervals, driven by pre-symptomatic transmission, have limited the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies for COVID-19, including contact tracing, case isolation, quarantine, and testing.
source: In the case of COVID-19, short generation intervals, driven by pre-symptomatic transmission, have limited the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies, including contact tracing (Ferretti et al., 2020b), case isolation, quarantine (Sun et al., 2020), and testing (Grassly et al., 2020; Johansson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining mitigation strategies.

claim: The generation- and serial-interval distributions can change over the course of an epidemic.
source: The generation- and serial-interval distributions can change over the course of an epidemic.
evidence: This is a general epidemiological principle supported by the subsequent explanation about mitigation measures.

claim: Generation and serial intervals are affected by the behavior of the population and can be shortened by the introduction of mitigation steps such as social distancing and case isolation.
source: For example, they are affected by the behavior of the population and can be shortened by the introduction of mitigation steps such as social distancing and case isolation, which limit the spread of the disease and reduce the probabilities of transmission after symptom onset (Ali et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ali et al., 2020.

claim: The mean forward serial interval stayed constant until around January 17, 2020, and then decreased gradually.
source: We found that the mean forward serial interval stayed constant until around the January 17, 2020, and then decreased gradually, indicating changes in transmission dynamics (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: A strict restriction on mobility (lockdown) imposed in Wuhan city on January 23 likely impacted generation and serial intervals of infectors who were infected a few days prior to this date.
source: In particular, a strict restrictions on mobility (lockdown) imposed in Wuhan city on January 23 (Kraemer et al., 2020) likely impacted generation (and therefore serial) intervals of infectors who were infected a few days prior to this date – for example, an individual who developed symptoms on January 23 would have had reduced transmission after January 23, thereby shortening their generation and serial intervals.
evidence: This claim combines a cited fact about the lockdown date with inference about its impact on transmission intervals.

claim: The negative trend in the mean serial interval from January 17–18 onward matches the timing of the decrease in the effective reproduction number R(t) for domestic cases in Wuhan, China.
source: The clear negative trend in the mean serial interval from January 17–18 onward also matches the timing of the decrease in the effective reproduction number R(t) for domestic cases in Wuhan, China, estimated by Lipsitch et al., 2020.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with estimates from Lipsitch et al., 2020.

claim: The dataset used for estimating the unmitigated generation-interval distribution includes 77 transmission pairs with a mean serial interval of 9.1 days (95% CI: 7.9–10.2) and a standard deviation of 5.2 days.
source: This dataset includes a total of 77 transmission pairs with a mean serial interval of 9.1 days (95% CI: 7.9–10.2), and a standard deviation of 5.2 days.
evidence: This claim presents descriptive statistics from the curated dataset.

claim: The unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a median of 7.9 days (95% CI: 6.8–9), a mean of 9.7 (95% CI: 8.3–11.2) days and standard deviation of 6.9 (95% CI: 4.3–10.1) days.
source: We estimate that the unmitigated generation-interval distribution has a median of 7.9 days (95% CI: 6.8–9), a mean of 9.7 (95% CI: 8.3–11.2) days and standard deviation of 6.9 (95% CI: 4.3–10.1) days.
evidence: This is the main result from the maximum likelihood analysis of the transmission pair data.

claim: The correlation parameter between incubation period and generation interval is estimated to be 0.75 (95% CI: 0.5–0.9).
source: Furthermore, we estimate a correlation parameter (see Methods) of 0.75 (95% CI: 0.5–0.9).
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the bivariate distribution analysis.

claim: The estimated mean generation interval is longer than the observed mean serial interval (9.1 days) of the period in question.
source: We note that our estimated mean generation interval is longer than the observed mean serial interval (9.1 days) of the period in question.
evidence: This is a comparison between the estimated and observed values from the analysis.

claim: During the exponential growth phase, the mean incubation period of the infectors is expected to be shorter than the mean incubation period of the infectee.
source: During the exponential growth phase, the mean incubation period of the infectors is expected to be shorter than the mean incubation period of the infectee – this effect causes the mean forward serial interval to become longer than the mean forward generation interval of the cohorts that developed symptoms during the study period.
evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding of epidemic dynamics and is supported by reference to Park et al., 2021.

claim: Approximately 20% (95% CI: 6–32%) of total transmission occurs pre-symptomatically.
source: The negative side of this distribution gives the pre-symptomatic transmission, which constitutes ≈20% (95% CI: 6–32%) of total transmission.
evidence: This is derived from the inferred bivariate distribution of incubation period and generation interval.

claim: The inferred generation-interval distribution has a heavier (right) tail compared to current available estimates.
source: A comparison with the current available estimates of the generation-interval distribution (Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020) reveals that the inferred distribution has a heavier (right) tail (Figure 4) and a higher median (7.9 days compared to 5.4–5.8 days) and standard deviation (6.9 days compared to 3.3–3.9 days).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous studies and visualization in Figure 4.

claim: About 18.5% (95% CI of 10–25%) of the transmission occurs after 14 days in the unmitigated scenario.
source: In contrast, our inferred generation-interval distribution predicts that about 18.5% (95% CI of 10–25%) of the transmission occurs after 14 days in the unmitigated scenario (assuming the behavior doesn't change due to quarantine, isolation, testing, etc.).
evidence: This is calculated from the inferred generation-interval distribution.

claim: The distributions of Ferretti et al., He et al., and Sun et al. indicate a residual fraction of transmission after 14 days of 2–4%.
source: The distributions of Ferretti et al., He et al., and Sun et al. indicate a residual fraction of transmission after 14 days of 2–4%, while the distribution assumed by Johansson et al. indicates only 0.2%.
evidence: This is a comparison with estimates from previous studies.

claim: The bias in previous estimates likely reflects the effects of mitigation steps and changes in awareness-driven behavior that prevent transmission during late stages of infection.
source: The bias in the previous estimates likely reflects the effects of mitigation steps, such as quarantine of exposed individuals, as well as changes in awareness-driven behavior, such as faster self-isolation after symptom onset, that prevent transmission during late stages of infection.
evidence: This is an inference about the causes of differences between the current study and previous estimates.

claim: Using late cutoff dates, such as January 21, leads to similar underestimation as seen in previous sources.
source: Our sensitivity analysis of the cutoff date for the period of unmitigated transmission indicates that using late cutoff dates, such as the January 21, leads to similar underestimation as seen in the previous sources.
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis presented in the study.

claim: On average, only approximately 20% (6–32%) of the unmitigated transmission happens before symptoms appear.
source: Our results suggest that, on average, only ≈20% (6–32%) of the unmitigated transmission happens before symptoms appear, lower than commonly stated values that already include mitigation effects (40–60% Ferretti et al., 2020a; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is derived from the bivariate distribution analysis and compared with previous estimates.

claim: The basic reproduction number R0 is estimated to be 2.2 with a CI of 1.9–2.7.
source: Combining our estimated generation-interval distribution with the early growth rate (Wallinga and Lipsitch, 2007), we find R0 to be 2.2 with a CI of 1.9–2.7 (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is calculated by combining the generation-interval distribution with the growth rate using the Euler-Lotka equation.

claim: The median generation interval of both the alpha and delta variants was estimated to be 6.7 days, 15% shorter than the original variant.
source: The median generation interval of both the alpha and delta variants was estimated to be 6.7 days, 15% shorter than the original variant.
evidence: This is an extrapolation based on viral kinetic information from Kissler et al., 2021.

claim: The median generation interval of the omicron variant was estimated to be 5.8 days, approximately 30% shorter than the original variant.
source: The median generation interval of the omicron variant was estimated to be 5.8 days, ≈30% shorter than the original variant.
evidence: This is an extrapolation based on viral kinetic information from Hay et al., 2022.

claim: More than 15–19% of the transmission potential occurs 5 days after symptoms for the three variants of concern in the absence of mitigation.
source: Even though these generation intervals are considerably shorter than the 7.9 days median generation intervals of the wild type, there might be a considerable amount of late transmission – for example, we estimate that more than 15–19% of the transmission potential occurs 5 days after symptoms for the three variants of concern (VOCs), in the absence of mitigation.
evidence: This is calculated from the extrapolated generation-interval distributions for VOCs.

claim: Individuals infected with the wild type still have, on average, approximately 18% of their transmission potential 14 days after infection.
source: The tail of the survival function (Figure 4B) indicates that individuals infected with the wild type still have, on average, ≈18% of their transmission potential 14 days after infection.
evidence: This is derived from the survival function of the generation-interval distribution shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A strong correlation exists between the incubation period and the generation interval.
source: We also found a strong correlation of the incubation period with the generation interval, accentuating the importance of quickly isolating individuals as soon as they show symptoms.
evidence: This is based on the estimated correlation parameter of 0.75 from the bivariate distribution analysis.

claim: The analysis by Johansson et al., 2021 underestimates the residual transmission after 10 days by an order of magnitude for the average individual (35% of the transmission vs. 4%).
source: As can be seen in Figure 4B, our results suggest that this analysis underestimates the residual transmission after 10 days by an order of magnitude for the average individual (35% of the transmission vs. 4%).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's results and those of Johansson et al., 2021, based on Figure 4B.

claim: Even when considering self-isolation of 70% of individuals immediately upon symptoms, there is a residual transmission of 11.8% compared to 1.3% in Johansson et al.'s estimates.
source: However, even when considering self-isolation of 70% of individuals immediately upon symptoms, as Johansson et al., 2021 assumed in their analysis, we still find a residual transmission of 11.8% compared to 1.3% in Johansson et al.'s estimates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated based on the generation-interval distribution and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The basic reproduction number R0 estimates derived in this study are close to reported values from early in the epidemic.
source: The basic reproduction number R0 estimates derived here are close to reported values from early in the epidemic value (Chinazzi et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020b), despite the longer estimate for the generation-interval distribution.
evidence: This is a comparison with R0 estimates from previous studies.

claim: The general shapes of the mean viral load trajectories and culture positivity, based on longitudinal studies, are comparable with the estimated unmitigated infectiousness profile.
source: Indeed, the general shapes of the mean viral load trajectories and culture positivity, based on longitudinal studies, are comparable with our estimated unmitigated infectiousness profile (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, comparison with Chu et al., 2022 ; Killingley et al., 2022; Kissler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with viral load data from other studies, shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The durations of infectiousness and incubation periods for the alpha and delta variants would be shorter by 15% relative to the original strain.
source: One prediction of our extrapolation procedure is that the durations of infectiousness and incubation periods for the alpha and delta variants would be shorter by 15% relative to the original strain, which is supported by independent studies (Brandal et al., 2021Grant et al., 2021; Hwang et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2021; Hart et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a prediction from the extrapolation method that is supported by citations to independent studies.

claim: Data on serial intervals were gathered from twelve relevant datasets identified through literature survey.
source: Twelve relevant datasets were identified: (Ali et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2020a; Xia et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhanwei et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology with citations to all source datasets.

claim: The combined dataset contained 2000 pairs, including duplicates.
source: In total, the combined dataset contained 2000 pairs, including duplicates.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic about the raw dataset before deduplication.

claim: After removing duplicates, 1002 transmission pairs remained in the dataset.
source: Lastly, we looked at the datasets not containing information regarding the sex and age of the cases (additional 406 pairs) and added to the dataset only pairs with symptom-onset dates that did not occur already in the first group (71 of the 406 cases were added, resulting in 1002 transmission pairs in total).
evidence: This describes the final dataset size after the deduplication process.

claim: The incubation period distribution was assumed to follow a lognormal distribution with a shape parameter of 0.53 and a scale parameter of 5.5 days.
source: The incubation period distribution was assumed to follow a lognormal distribution with a shape parameter of 0.53 and a scale parameter of 5.5 days, following Xin et al., 2021.
evidence: This describes a methodological assumption based on a previous meta-analysis.

claim: The daily growth rates in the early outbreak period in Wuhan and in the rest of China were estimated to be r=0.08 day⁻¹ and r=0.10 day⁻¹, respectively.
source: The daily growth rates in the early outbreak period in Wuhan in particular and in the rest of China were estimated by another study (Tsang et al., 2020) to be r=0.08 day–1 and r=0.10 day–1 , respectively.
evidence: This cites growth rate estimates from Tsang et al., 2020.

claim: Most available estimates of the generation-interval distribution did not fully account for mitigation effects such as contact tracing and case isolation.
source: Most available estimates of the generation-interval distribution addressed the effects of mitigation only in a limited manner, not fully accounting for steps such as contact tracing and case isolation (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of previous studies with citations.

claim: The distribution of realized serial intervals depends on the rate of the spread of the disease as well as the direction from which they are measured.
source: First, the distribution of realized serial intervals depends on the rate of the spread of the disease as well as the direction from which they are measured: either forward from a cohort of infectors who developed symptoms at the same time or backward from a cohort of infectees (Park et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a methodological issue in serial interval estimation, supported by citation to Park et al., 2021.

claim: When the incidence of infection is increasing, recently infected individuals represent a bigger fraction of the population and are over-represented in cohorts of individuals who develop symptoms on a given day.
source: When the incidence of infection is increasing, recently infected individuals represent a bigger fraction of this population and thus are over-represented in this cohort.
evidence: This explains a statistical bias that occurs during epidemic growth, based on epidemiological theory.

claim: Most analyses of serial-interval distributions assume that the incubation periods of the infector and infectee follow the same distribution.
source: However, most analyses of serial-interval distributions assume that the incubation periods of the infector and infectee follow the same distribution (Ganyani et al., 2020; He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020), and only a few studies partially account for this dynamical bias (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of methodological assumptions in previous studies with citations.

claim: Incubation periods and temporal profile of infectiousness are likely to be correlated across infectors.
source: Second, incubation periods and temporal profile of infectiousness are likely to be correlated across infectors – that is, individuals that show symptoms later or earlier are also more likely to infect others later or earlier, respectively.
evidence: This describes an expected biological correlation that is a key consideration in the modeling approach.

claim: Most available studies make strict assumptions on the relationship between the incubation period and the generation interval.
source: Most available studies make strict assumptions on the relationship between the incubation period and the generation interval – either assuming that they are independent (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Ganyani et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020) or that the time from onset of symptoms to transmission (TOST) is independent of the incubation period (He et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of methodological assumptions in previous studies with citations.

claim: Biases can arise from the data collection process, such as determining who infected whom based on symptom-onset dates, which can miss pre-symptomatic transmission.
source: Finally, biases can arise from the data collection process. For example, determining who infected whom based on their symptom-onset dates can miss pre-symptomatic transmission.
evidence: This describes a potential source of bias in transmission pair data collection.

claim: Long serial intervals may represent multiple chains of transmissions where intermediate hosts were not correctly identified.
source: Likewise, long serial intervals may represent multiple chains of transmissions where intermediate hosts were not correctly identified.
evidence: This describes another potential source of bias in transmission pair data.

claim: These biases can cause overestimation of the mean serial interval as well as the mean generation interval.
source: These biases can cause overestimation of the mean serial interval as well as the mean generation interval.
evidence: This is an inference about the direction of bias from data collection issues.

claim: The mean serial interval for the early period of the epidemic was 7.8 days (95% CI: 7–8.6 days) according to Ali et al., 2020.
source: Although this is substantially longer than the mean of 7.8 days (95% CI: 7–8.6 days) suggested by Ali et al., 2020, for the early period of the epidemic, there is considerable uncertainty in both estimates with overlapping CI.
evidence: This cites a previous estimate from Ali et al., 2020.

claim: Other studies that did not differentiate different stages of the epidemic estimated a much lower mean serial interval (4–6 days).
source: Other studies that did not differentiate different stages of the epidemic estimated a much lower mean serial interval (4–6 days) (He et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Zhanwei et al., 2020).
evidence: This summarizes estimates from multiple previous studies with citations.

claim: The incubation period distribution has a mean of 6.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.6 days according to Xin et al., 2021.
source: We used the maximum likelihood framework to estimate the parameters of the joint bivariate distribution of the generation interval and the incubation period, assuming a known incubation period distribution (Xin et al., 2021) with a mean of 6.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.6 days.
evidence: This cites the incubation period distribution parameters from Xin et al., 2021.

claim: The model was able to fit the observed serial-interval data well with or without the growth rate adjustment.
source: With or without the growth rate adjustment, the model was able to fit the observed serial-interval data well (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the goodness of fit of the model, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Changing the assumed growth rate during the early outbreak period had very little effect on the results.
source: Changing the assumed growth rate during this period had very little effect on the results, with estimated mean increasing from 9.5 to 9.7 days, as assumed growth rates decreased from 0.16 to 0.04 day–1 (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days had very little effect on the results.
source: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days (Appendix 1—figure 10), as well as inclusion of severe cases in the dataset (Appendix 1—figure 11) had very little effect.
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 10.

claim: Inclusion of severe cases in the dataset had very little effect on the results.
source: Changing the incubation period to one with a median in the range of 4–5.5 days (Appendix 1—figure 10), as well as inclusion of severe cases in the dataset (Appendix 1—figure 11) had very little effect.
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11.

claim: Removing the transmission pairs with the highest serial intervals from the dataset caused a small decrease in the generation-interval distribution.
source: The sensitivity analysis to high serial-interval values caused a slight decrease in the mean generation interval, but still resulted in a wide distribution. Removing the transmission pairs with the highest serial intervals from the dataset caused a small decrease in the generation-interval distribution.
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis.

claim: For a removal of the top 10% values, the inferred distribution has a median of 7.2 days and a mean of 8.3 days.
source: For a removal of the top 10% values, the inferred distribution has a median of 7.2 days and a mean of 8.3 days (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Switching the order of some of the transmission pairs caused a decrease in both the median and mean of the generation interval, as well as a decrease in the correlation parameter.
source: Switching the order of some of the transmission pairs caused a decrease in both the median and mean of the generation interval, as well as a decrease in the correlation parameter (Figure 5G–I, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Even when reordering 10% of the pairs the distribution is wide, with the median of bootstrap estimates for the median generation interval being 7.2 days.
source: However, even when reordering 10% of the pairs the distribution is wide: for example, the median of bootstrap estimates for the median generation interval is 7.2 days (Figure 5H).
evidence: This describes results from sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The unmitigated generation-interval distribution is likely wider than previously thought.
source: These sensitivity analyses demonstrate the robustness of our conclusion: the unmitigated generation-interval distribution is likely wider than previously thought.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sensitivity analyses.

claim: The cutoff date seems to be the dominant factor in the analysis, meaning that taking the effects of interventions into account is the most important for an accurate estimate of the generation-interval distribution.
source: We conclude that the cutoff date seems to be the dominant factor in our analysis, presumably meaning that taking the effects of interventions into account is the most important for an accurate estimate of the generation-interval distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different sensitivity analyses.

claim: Superspreading likely had negligible effects on the analysis because the data included at most two events with more than two infectees (4 and 7).
source: However, the data we chose to include in the analysis consisted of at most two events with more than two infectees (4 and 7), and therefore superspreading likely had negligible effects on our analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the dataset.

claim: When mitigation strategies are introduced, the amount of post-symptomatic transmission is expected to decrease, leading to an increase in the fraction of pre-symptomatic transmission.
source: When mitigation strategies are introduced, we would expect the amount of post-symptomatic transmission to decrease, leading to an increase in the fraction of pre-symptomatic transmission.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the effects of mitigation on transmission timing.

claim: The estimate of the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission is lower than previous estimates that looked at a later period.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that our estimate of the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission is lower than previous estimates that looked at a later period (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous estimates with citations, explained by the timing of data collection.

claim: The results match the trend shown by Sun et al., 2020, in which faster isolation of cases increases the pre-symptomatic fraction of transmission and shortens the mean generation interval.
source: Furthermore, our results match the trend shown by Sun et al., 2020, in which the faster isolation of cases increases the pre-symptomatic fraction of transmission and shortens the mean generation interval.
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Sun et al., 2020.

claim: Both the bivariate lognormal model and the adjusted logistic TOST model estimate large means and standard deviations of the generation intervals, and a low proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission for the current dataset.
source: Both models estimate large means and standard deviations of the generation intervals, and a low proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission for the current dataset.
evidence: This describes results from comparing two different modeling approaches.

claim: Applying both models to the data from Ferretti et al., 2020a, produced similar distributions with lower estimates for the mean generation interval and higher per-symptomatic proportion.
source: Applying both models to the data from Ferretti et al., 2020a, produced similar distributions with lower estimates for the mean generation interval and higher per-symptomatic proportion (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This describes results from applying the models to a different dataset, shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The results presented in this study are a product of the focus on the data prior to mitigation steps, in combination with the correction for the growth of the epidemic.
source: This indicates that the results presented in this study are a product of the focus on the data prior to mitigation steps, in combination with the correction for the growth of the epidemic.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the key factors contributing to the study's findings.

claim: Transmission pairs data can be prone to incorrect identification of transmission pairs, including the direction of transmission.
source: Transmission pairs data can be prone to incorrect identification of transmission pairs, including the direction of transmission.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the data type used in the study.

claim: Pre-symptomatic transmission can cause infectors to develop symptoms after their infectees, making it difficult to identify who infected whom.
source: In particular, pre-symptomatic transmission can cause infectors to develop symptoms after their infectees, making it difficult to identify who infected whom.
evidence: This describes a specific challenge in identifying transmission pairs.

claim: Data from the early outbreak might be sensitive to ascertainment and reporting biases which could lead to missing links in transmission pairs.
source: Data from the early outbreak might also be sensitive to ascertainment and reporting biases which could lead to missing links in transmission pairs, causing serial intervals to appear longer (e.g., people who transmit asymptomatically might not be identified).
evidence: This describes potential biases in early outbreak data.

claim: When multiple potential infectors are present, an individual who developed symptoms close to when the infectee became infected is more likely to be identified as the infector.
source: Moreover, when multiple potential infectors are present, an individual who developed symptoms close to when the infectee became infected is more likely to be identified as the infector.
evidence: This describes a potential ascertainment bias in transmission pair identification.

claim: These biases might increase the estimated correlation of the incubation period and the period of infectiousness.
source: These biases might increase the estimated correlation of the incubation period and the period of infectiousness.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential effect of ascertainment biases on parameter estimates.

claim: The relatively narrow ranges of uncertainty suggest that the results are not very sensitive to specific transmission pairs data points being included in the analysis.
source: The relatively narrow ranges of uncertainty suggest that the results are not very sensitive to specific transmission pairs data points being included in the analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bootstrapping results.

claim: Although potential biases can decrease the inferred mean generation interval, the main conclusions about the long unmitigated generation intervals remained robust.
source: The sensitivity analysis shows that although these potential biases can decrease the inferred mean generation interval, our main conclusions about the long unmitigated generation intervals (high median length and substantial residual transmission after 14 days) remained robust (Figure 5).
evidence: This summarizes the findings from sensitivity analyses shown in Figure 5.

claim: It is nearly impossible to find two completely unrelated datasets from the period prior to mitigation, limiting the ability of further validation of the current results.
source: Due to the nature of early spread of a new unknown disease, it is nearly impossible to find two completely unrelated datasets from the period prior to mitigation, limiting the ability of further validation of the current results.
evidence: This describes a limitation in validating the study's findings.

claim: Without testing, the residual transmission after quarantine would be substantially higher than previous estimates suggest.
source: Indeed, the unmitigated infectiousness profile suggests that without testing, the residual transmission after quarantine would be substantially higher – thus supporting the policy of requiring PCR or rapid tests for ending quarantines, as required in many countries.
evidence: This is an inference about policy implications based on the estimated generation-interval distribution.

claim: Quarantine and isolation measures typically begin several days after the infection event, suggesting that the actual amount of post-quarantine and isolation transmission would be lower than estimated.
source: In addition, quarantine and isolation measures typically begin several days after the infection event, suggesting that the actual amount of post-quarantine and isolation transmission would be lower than what we estimate.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical application of the estimates.

claim: The R0 estimates are close to reported values from early in the epidemic despite the longer estimate for the generation-interval distribution, mainly due to using the corrected growth rate.
source: This is mainly due to using the corrected growth rate, which is considerably lower than previously assumed values (Tsang et al., 2020).
evidence: This explains why R0 estimates are similar to previous estimates despite different generation intervals.

claim: The nature of the relationship between viral load, culture positivity, symptom onset, and real-world infectivity is complex and not well characterized.
source: However, the nature of the relationship between viral load, culture positivity, symptom onset, and real-world infectivity is complex and not well characterized.
evidence: This describes a limitation in using viral load data to infer infectiousness.

claim: The ability to infer infectiousness from viral load data is very limited, especially near the tail of infectiousness, several days following symptom onset and peak viral loads.
source: Therefore, the ability to infer infectiousness from viral load data is very limited, especially near the tail of infectiousness, several days following symptom onset and peak viral loads.
evidence: This describes a limitation in using viral load data for inferring late-stage infectiousness.

claim: Viral load models are usually made to fit the measurements during an initial exponential clearance phase and in many cases miss a later slow decay.
source: Viral load models are usually made to fit the measurements during an initial exponential clearance phase and in many cases miss a later slow decay (Kissler et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a limitation of viral load models, citing Kissler et al., 2021.

claim: There is considerable individual-level variation in viral trajectories that isn't accounted for in population-mean models.
source: Furthermore, there is considerable individual-level variation in viral trajectories that isn't accounted for in population-mean models (Kissler et al., 2021; Singanayagam et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a limitation of population-level viral load models, with citations.

claim: The extrapolation of new VOCs' infectiousness is restricted to a single parameter characterizing the viral duration of clearance to avoid over-interpretation of viral load data.
source: Due to these caveats and in order to avoid over-interpretation of viral load data, we restrict our extrapolation of new VOCs' infectiousness to a single parameter characterizing the viral duration of clearance.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice made to address limitations in viral load data.

claim: Analyses of generation- and serial-interval distributions of new variants are necessarily subject to behavioral and intervention effects and are likely to underestimate the true duration of SARS-CoV-2 infectiousness.
source: Although a few studies have tried to characterize generation- and serial-interval distributions of new variants (Hart et al., 2021; Pung et al., 2021; Ryu et al., 2021; Hart et al., 2022), these analyses are necessarily subject to behavioral and intervention effects and are likely to underestimate the true duration of SARS-CoV-2 infectiousness.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of studies on variant generation intervals, with citations.

claim: The estimates of residual transmission suggest that caution is needed with the CDC's newly updated isolation guideline in the absence of additional measures such as testing.
source: Our estimates of residual transmission (more than 15% transmission occurring at least 5 days after symptom onset for the alpha, delta, and omicron variants) suggest that caution is needed with the CDC's newly updated (CDC, 2021) isolation guideline in the absence of additional measures, such as testing, before releasing isolated individuals.
evidence: This is a policy implication drawn from the extrapolated generation-interval distributions for VOCs.

claim: Compartmentalization in the respiratory tract, aerosolization, receptor binding affinity, and immune history can play important roles in determining the infectiousness profiles of SARS-CoV-2 variants.
source: Moreover, compartmentalization in the respiratory tract, aerosolization, receptor binding affinity, and immune history can also play important roles in determining the infectiousness profiles of SARS-CoV-2 variants (Puhach et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes additional factors that can affect infectiousness, citing Puhach et al., 2022.

claim: Changes in population-level susceptibility can cause the generation-interval distribution to change over time.
source: Furthermore, changes in population-level susceptibility can also cause the generation-interval distribution to change over time (Kenah et al., 2008; Champredon and Dushoff, 2015).
evidence: This describes a factor that can affect generation intervals over time, with citations.

claim: The extrapolations are necessarily crude given the complex relationship between viral load, symptomaticity, and infectiousness.
source: Our extrapolations are necessarily crude given the complex relationship between viral load, symptomaticity, and infectiousness discussed above.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the extrapolation approach.

claim: The estimates don't take into account the effect of current interventions and behavioral changes.
source: Our analysis focuses on estimating unmitigated intervals. Therefore, our estimates don't take into account the effect of current interventions and behavioral changes.
evidence: This describes a limitation in the applicability of the estimates.

claim: The estimates can be useful for assessing isolation and contact tracing measures.
source: Nonetheless, these estimates can be useful for assessing isolation and contact tracing measures.
evidence: This describes a potential application of the unmitigated estimates.

claim: With the emergence of new VOCs, future studies could use the framework presented to update estimates of the generation-interval distributions for emerging strains.
source: Furthermore, with the emergence of new VOCs, which may exhibit altered transmission dynamics than previously dominant wild type (Kissler et al., 2021), future studies could use our framework to update estimates of the generation-interval distributions for these emerging strains even under mitigation conditions and with inference of the correlation to the incubation period.
evidence: This describes a potential future application of the study's framework.

claim: The analysis provides a view of the infectiousness profile of an infected individual in absence of mitigation steps, which is a key ingredient of many models used for guiding policy.
source: Our analysis provides a view of the infectiousness profile of an infected individual in absence of mitigation steps, which is a key ingredient of many models used for guiding policy.
evidence: This summarizes the main contribution of the study.

claim: The results demonstrate the importance of considering possible biases in the serial-interval data used for estimating the generation-interval distribution.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate the importance of considering possible biases in the serial-interval data used for estimating the generation-interval distribution, as well as the underlying assumptions made when estimating the distribution from the source data.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological implications of the study.

claim: Kissler et al. estimated exponential growth and clearance rates of viral load trajectories across 173 participants from the National Basketball Association between November 28, 2020, and August 11, 2021.
source: Kissler et al. estimated exponential growth and clearance (decay) rates of viral load trajectories across 173 participants from the National Basketball Association between November 28, 2020, and August 11, 2021, including individuals infected by alpha and delta variants.
evidence: This describes the data source used for extrapolating VOC generation intervals.

claim: Hay et al. extended the viral load analysis to include an additional 204 individuals who were infected by delta or omicron variants.
source: Hay et al. extended the analysis to include an additional 204 individuals who were infected by delta or omicron variants.
evidence: This describes an additional data source used for extrapolating VOC generation intervals.

claim: Studies showed that the overall viral shedding time of the new variants was shorter than the non-VOCs, mainly due to a significant reduction of the clearance time.
source: These studies showed that the overall viral shedding time of the new variants was shorter than the non-VOCs, mainly due to a significant reduction of the clearance time – the duration of the period from the peak viral load back to undetectable level of viral load.
evidence: This summarizes findings from Kissler et al. and Hay et al. about VOC viral kinetics.

claim: The group of non-VOCs is assumed to represent the original wild-type variant.
source: Following Kissler et al., we assume that the group of non-VOCs represents the original wild-type variant.
evidence: This describes an assumption made in the extrapolation method.

claim: Differences in clearance durations reflect biological differences in the rate in which the variant infects the host.
source: We assume that differences in clearance durations reflect biological differences in the rate in which the variant infects the host, and therefore base the extrapolation on the ratio of clearance durations
evidence: This describes an assumption underlying the extrapolation method.

claim: Previously inferred viral load trajectories qualitatively match the shape of the distribution of transmission probability as a function of the TOST.
source: Although the connection of viral load levels and infectiousness is not well characterized, previously inferred viral load trajectories qualitatively match the shape of the distribution of transmission probability as a function of the TOST, providing support for our approximation (Figure 6).
evidence: This provides justification for using viral load trajectories to extrapolate infectiousness, shown in Figure 6.

claim: This apparent similarity between viral load trajectories and transmission probability was demonstrated in previous studies.
source: This apparent similarity was also demonstrated in previous studies (He et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2021; Marc et al., 2021).
evidence: This cites previous studies that support the relationship between viral load and infectiousness.
